```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
has_nestimate <- requireNamespace("Nestimate", quietly = TRUE)
```

A network statistic is only as trustworthy as its implementation. The
similarity measures used to normalize co-occurrence counts have short
formulas (van Eck & Waltman, 2009), but an implementation has to make many
small decisions around them: how a transaction that lists an item twice is
counted, whether the diagonal of the matrix holds item frequencies or zeros,
which items survive a frequency filter, and in which order a threshold and a
normalization are applied. Two implementations that agree on the formulas
can still disagree on the numbers.

**Nestimate** contains an independent implementation of the same eight
similarity measures in its own `cooccurrence()` function, written for its
network-estimation framework. This guide compares the two on the data
bundled with **cooccure** and shows that, once two documented conventions are
aligned, they return the same weight matrix for every measure. The same
comparison is kept in the package repository
(`tests/equivalence/test-nestimate-equivalence.R`) and runs in continuous
integration, on hand-built inputs in all five input formats both packages
read, with frequency and weight filters, and on 40 randomly generated
networks, so that the two cannot drift apart unnoticed. It is not part of
the tests shipped to CRAN, so that a change in one package cannot fail the
other's check.

```{r package}
library(cooccure)
```

Both packages export a function called `cooccurrence()`, and they return
different classes. **Nestimate** is therefore not attached here; every call
to it is written as `Nestimate::cooccurrence()`.

```{r version, eval = has_nestimate}
packageVersion("Nestimate")
```

The comparison below was rendered against this version of **Nestimate**.

## Data

Two bundled tables, in two input formats, supply the networks:

- **`movies`**, a delimited format: one row per film, with the column
  `genres` holding the film's genres separated by commas. Genres are the
  items and films the transactions; 1,000 films, 22 genres.
- **`actors`**, a long format: one row per actor and film, with `actor` as
  the item and the film identifier `tconst` as the transaction; 624 actors in
  401 films.

## Two helpers that return comparable matrices

The two packages store their networks differently: **cooccure** returns an
edge list whose matrix is read with `as_matrix()`, and **Nestimate** returns a
`netobject` that holds the matrix. The first helper returns the **cooccure**
matrix; the second returns the **Nestimate** matrix with the diagonal set to
zero, since **cooccure** never stores self co-occurrence.

```{r helpers}
cooccure_matrix <- function(...) {
  as_matrix(cooccure::cooccurrence(...))
}

nestimate_matrix <- function(..., diagonal = FALSE) {
  m <- as.matrix(Nestimate::cooccurrence(..., diagonal = diagonal)$weights)
  diag(m) <- 0
  m
}
```

A third helper aligns the two matrices on their item names and returns the
largest absolute difference between any two cells, and a fourth applies it to
every similarity measure, returning one row per measure.

```{r compare-helpers}
max_difference <- function(a, b) {
  items <- sort(rownames(a))
  stopifnot("the two networks hold different items" =
              setequal(rownames(a), rownames(b)))
  max(abs(a[items, items] - b[items, items]))
}

compare_measures <- function(...) {
  measures <- c("none", "jaccard", "cosine", "inclusion", "association",
                "dice", "equivalence", "relative")
  rows <- lapply(measures, function(s) {
    a <- cooccure_matrix(..., similarity = s)
    b <- nestimate_matrix(..., similarity = s)
    data.frame(similarity = s, items = nrow(a),
               max_abs_difference = max_difference(a, b))
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
```

## Do the two packages agree on every similarity measure?

The genre network of the `movies` table is built with each of the eight
measures by both packages, and the matrices are compared cell by cell.

```{r genres, eval = has_nestimate}
compare_measures(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",")
```

Both packages find the same 22 genres for every measure. Seven of the eight
measures agree exactly; for `cosine` the largest difference is of the order
of 10<sup>-17</sup>, which is floating-point rounding from computing a square
root in a different order, far below any meaningful difference in a
similarity between 0 and 1.

The actor network is larger, 624 items and more than 4,000 edges, and comes
from a long table rather than a delimited column.

```{r actors, eval = has_nestimate}
compare_measures(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst")
```

The result is the same: every measure agrees to within 10<sup>-15</sup>, and
`cosine` is again the only one with a non-zero difference.

## Do filters give the same network?

Frequency and weight filters are where implementations most often part ways,
because a filter can be applied before or after normalization. Here only
genres in at least 20 films are kept, and Jaccard weights below 0.1 are
dropped.

```{r filters, eval = has_nestimate}
max_difference(
  cooccure_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                  similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 20, threshold = 0.1),
  nestimate_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                   similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 20, threshold = 0.1)
)
```

The filtered networks are identical: both packages remove rare items before
counting and apply the weight threshold after the similarity measure.

## Where the conventions differ

Two documented conventions differ between the packages, and both must be
aligned before the numbers can match.

### The diagonal

By default **Nestimate** stores each item's frequency on the diagonal of the
matrix (`diagonal = TRUE`), while **cooccure** always sets it to zero. For
seven measures this changes only the diagonal, which the helper above zeroes.
For `relative` it changes every cell: `relative` divides each row by its sum,
and with the diagonal kept, the item's own frequency is part of that sum.

```{r diagonal, eval = has_nestimate}
max_difference(
  cooccure_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                  similarity = "relative"),
  nestimate_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                   similarity = "relative", diagonal = TRUE)
)
```

With the diagonal kept, the off-diagonal `relative` weights differ by up to
0.5. With `diagonal = FALSE`, as in the comparisons above, they agree
exactly. The two packages therefore implement the same measure; the
difference is in which co-occurrences count toward an item's total.

### Ties at the `top_n` cut

`top_n` keeps the heaviest edges. When several edges tie at the cut,
**cooccure** truncates to exactly `top_n` edges and **Nestimate** keeps every
edge tied with the last one. In the genre network, three pairs have an
inclusion weight of 1, so the two packages return a different number of
edges for `top_n = 1`.

```{r ties, eval = has_nestimate}
cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
             similarity = "inclusion", top_n = 3)
```

These are the three tied pairs. With `top_n = 1`, **cooccure** keeps the first
of them and **Nestimate** keeps all three; the edges **cooccure** keeps are
always a subset of those **Nestimate** keeps, with the same weights.

### Direction of `relative`

`relative` is the only asymmetric measure: the weight from genre A to genre
B is the share of A's co-occurrences that involve B, which is not the share
of B's co-occurrences that involve A. Both packages store the asymmetric
matrix compared above. **cooccure** returns one edge per direction and marks
the network as directed, and so does **Nestimate** from version 1.0.11 onward.

```{r relative, eval = has_nestimate}
genre_shares <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                             similarity = "relative")
print(genre_shares, n = 4)
```

The header reports directed edges: the 129 genre pairs give 258 directed
edges. The strongest runs from Western to Drama with a weight of 1, because
the single Western film is also tagged Drama and nothing else. The two
directions of one pair can differ widely, as the Drama and Romance pair
shows.

```{r relative-pair, eval = has_nestimate}
subset(as.data.frame(genre_shares),
       from %in% c("Drama", "Romance") & to %in% c("Drama", "Romance"))
```

More than half (0.553) of Romance's co-occurrences are with Drama, but only
0.161 of Drama's co-occurrences are with Romance, because Drama co-occurs
with almost every other genre. The raw count, 131 films, is the same in both
directions.

## What the comparison covers

The comparison establishes that, given the same transactions, the two
packages compute the same weights. It does not test input parsing that only
one package offers, such as the sliding windows, attention counting, event
logs and `aggregate_by` of **cooccure**; those are checked in
`tests/testthat/test-cooccurrence.R` against values computed by hand. For the
choice between the measures themselves, see the
[guide to similarity measures](similarity-measures.html).

## References

van Eck, N. J., & Waltman, L. (2009). How to normalize cooccurrence data? An
analysis of some well-known similarity measures. *Journal of the American
Society for Information Science and Technology*, 60(8), 1635–1651.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.21075>
